facts.text: ISO 12100 is the foundation standard for machine safety: it defines basic terms such as hazard, risk and protective measure and establishes a general method for reducing machine risk in a fixed order.
facts.quote: ISO 12100 is the foundation standard for machine safety: it defines the basic words (hazard, risk, protective measure) and sets out the general method for reducing machine risk in a fixed order.

facts.text: Machinery standards have three layers: Type-A standards provide basic concepts and the general method, and ISO 12100 is a Type-A standard.
facts.quote: Machinery standards come in three layers. Type-A standards give basic concepts and the general method; ISO 12100 is the type-A standard.

facts.text: Type-B machinery standards cover one safety aspect or safeguard for many machines; ISO 13849 is an example covering control systems.
facts.quote: Type-B standards cover one safety aspect or safeguard for many machines, such as ISO 13849 for control systems.

facts.text: Type-C machinery standards cover one machine type in detail and take precedence; ISO 21815-3 for collision systems on earth-moving machines is a Type-C standard under ISO 12100.
facts.quote: Type-C standards cover one machine type in detail and take precedence; ISO 21815-3 for collision systems on earth-moving machines is a type-C standard under ISO 12100 [Chapter 3].

facts.text: The ISO 12100 method starts with risk assessment: set the limits of the machine and its use, identify hazards, and estimate and evaluate risk.
facts.quote: First, a risk assessment: set the limits of the machine and its use, identify hazards, estimate and evaluate the risk.

facts.text: ISO 12100 risk reduction follows three steps in strict order: inherently safe design, safeguarding and complementary protective measures, then information for use.
facts.quote: Second, risk reduction in three steps in strict order.

facts.text: The first ISO 12100 risk-reduction step, inherently safe design, removes or reduces hazards by design, for example through lower speeds or better operator visibility.
facts.quote: Inherently safe design comes first: remove or reduce the hazard by design, for example lower speeds or better operator visibility.

facts.text: The second ISO 12100 risk-reduction step is safeguarding and complementary protective measures, including guards, sensors and functions such as automatic braking.
facts.quote: Safeguarding and complementary protective measures come second: guards, sensors, and functions such as automatic braking.

facts.text: The third ISO 12100 risk-reduction step is information for use, including warnings, instructions and training; residual risk is the risk remaining after risk reduction.
facts.quote: Information for use comes third: warnings, instructions and training. Residual risk is what remains.

facts.text: The booklet reports that the EU Machinery Regulation requires risk reduction, safe and reliable control systems, and technical evidence of conformity.
facts.quote: the EU Machinery Regulation requires risk reduction, safe and reliable control systems and technical evidence of conformity [Chapter 3]

facts.text: ISO 20474 and EN 474 provide baseline safety requirements for earth-moving machinery.
facts.quote: ISO 20474 and EN 474 give baseline safety requirements for earth-moving machinery

facts.text: The EN 474:2022 family was designated in Great Britain in August 2026.
facts.quote: the EN 474:2022 family designated in Great Britain in August 2026 [Chapter 3]

facts.text: The mining industry's nine-layer model follows the ISO 12100 logic: site design and operating controls at Levels 1 to 7 are to be understood before adding advisory technology at Level 8 and intervention technology at Level 9.
facts.quote: site design and operating controls (Levels 1 to 7) are to be understood before advisory (Level 8) and intervention (Level 9) technology is added [Chapter 1].

facts.text: Under ISO 12100, automatic braking comes after inherently safe design and operates within the site's other controls; the same braking algorithm therefore gives different safety results at sites with different traffic rules and pedestrian controls.
facts.quote: In ISO 12100 logic it comes after inherently safe design and sits inside the site's other controls, which is why the same braking algorithm gives different safety results at sites with different traffic rules and pedestrian controls [Chapter 1].
